title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 87–88
description: Advanced English suffixes, compound modifiers, classical roots, derivation, and lexical blends, with usage and register distinctions.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study based on a user-provided book. Vocabulary targets are selected from source teaching pages, exercises, and answer-key entries; all examples, translations, and usage notes are independently authored. Original exercises and extended passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Units 87–88 teaching sections A–B, morphology/Language help notes, exercises 87.1–87.6 and 88.1–88.5, and their respective answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied for short targets only where reasonably confident; blank IPA is used rather than guess. Longer compounds may have blank IPA; no connected-speech transcript is implied.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing text is in English apart from Brazilian Portuguese translations inside pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Teaching pages and exercise answer key were checked for meaningful vocabulary targets, grammatical patterns and source attribution. Original examples and translations were reviewed. JSON schema parity, fields, unique IDs and static TTS target rules were checked programmatically.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 audio. Browser import, text-to-speech performance and speech recognition were not tested. Some classical roots are analytical clues, not productive templates for inventing new vocabulary.

units.title: Unit 87 — Suffixes: forming new words
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 180–181 (PDF pages 182–183).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Word formation · productive suffixes and word-class contrasts
learningObjectives: Recognise productive suffixes and interpret compound adjectives using their roots and suffix meanings.
Apply singular-noun patterns in compound modifiers and distinguish suffixes that form different word classes.
Use exercise-derived formations appropriately in advanced written and spoken English.

sectionsChecked: A · Productive suffixes and morphology guidance
B · Suffixes in different word classes

items.example: This jacket is washable at thirty degrees.
items.note: The productive suffix -able forms adjectives meaning able to be washed or otherwise acted on.

items.example: The clinic uses disposable gloves for routine examinations.
items.note: Disposable means designed to be thrown away after use; the base verb is dispose.

items.example: The outcome was remarkably predictable once the results were published.
items.note: Predictable means capable of being anticipated; often evaluates behaviour or results.

items.example: Several delays were avoidable with better planning.
items.note: An avoidable problem could have been prevented.

items.example: The revised schedule made the workload manageable.
items.note: A manageable situation or task is possible to deal with successfully.

items.pt: preocupado com a saúde; atento à saúde
items.example: Health-conscious consumers often check nutritional labels.
items.note: -conscious describes someone who gives particular attention to an aspect of life.

items.pt: atento às classes sociais; consciente das diferenças de classe
items.example: The novel depicts a highly class-conscious society.
items.note: Describes strong awareness of social class and status.

items.example: A safety-conscious employer checks procedures before commissioning equipment.
items.note: Usually a singular noun precedes -conscious; not safeties-conscious.

items.pt: atento ao tempo; preocupado com prazos
items.example: The time-conscious organiser kept every speaker within the allotted slot.
items.note: Focuses on punctuality, efficiency and time constraints.

items.example: They hoped for a stress-free journey after weeks of preparation.
items.note: -free indicates the absence of something undesirable.

items.example: The airport has a tax-free shopping area.
items.note: The compound indicates that the relevant tax is not charged in the context stated.

items.example: The company markets additive-free foods to health-conscious customers.
items.note: Indicates no additives; often modifies food or drink.

items.example: A fibre-rich diet can include vegetables and whole grains.
items.note: -rich indicates a high content of the named substance; British spelling fibre.

items.example: The nutritionist recommended several calcium-rich foods.
items.note: Often used in descriptions of nutrients and diets.

items.example: The council funded a community-led housing initiative.
items.note: -led names the controlling or initiating group; use a singular community before led.

items.example: A student-led protest prompted a meeting with university officials.
items.note: Identifies who directs the action, not merely who attends it.

items.example: The factory adopted a worker-led safety programme.
items.note: Describes a programme or movement directed by workers.

items.pt: com ideias semelhantes; de mentalidade parecida
items.example: She joined a group of like-minded researchers.
items.note: Often modifies people who share interests or beliefs.

items.pt: focado na carreira; orientado à carreira
items.example: The career-minded graduates sought internships abroad.
items.note: Describes someone who prioritises career advancement.

items.example: His money-minded approach overlooked the project's social impact.
items.note: Can be disapproving; not always a neutral compliment.

items.example: The proposal sounded high-minded but lacked a practical budget.
items.note: Means guided by high moral standards or ideals; may sometimes be sceptical.

items.pt: próprio para forno; resistente ao calor do forno
items.example: Pour the mixture into an ovenproof dish.
items.note: -proof describes resistance to a particular cause of harm or difficulty.

items.example: The technician kept the documents in a waterproof pouch.
items.note: Resists water penetration; not equivalent to water-resistant in every context.

items.pt: à prova de som; com isolamento acústico
items.example: They installed a soundproof booth for recording interviews.
items.note: Prevents or greatly reduces sound transmission.

items.pt: extremamente fácil de usar; à prova de erros comuns
items.example: The team wanted idiot-proof setup instructions.
items.note: Informal and potentially insulting; use user-friendly in considerate professional writing.

items.example: The study examined stress-related absences from work.
items.note: The first noun is generally singular before -related.

items.example: Some age-related changes are gradual rather than sudden.
items.note: Indicates association with age without necessarily claiming direct causation.

items.example: She felt guilt-ridden after withholding important information.
items.note: -ridden suggests being burdened or overwhelmed by something negative.

items.example: Residents wanted more investment in the crime-ridden neighbourhood.
items.note: Usually negative, referring to high levels of crime.

items.example: After the operation he was bedridden for several days.
items.note: A lexicalised compound describing someone obliged to remain in bed through illness or injury.

items.pt: digno de virar notícia; de interesse jornalístico
items.example: The discovery was newsworthy because it challenged earlier findings.
items.note: -worthy means deserving or meriting the named response.

items.example: Her careful handling of the complaint was praiseworthy.
items.note: Indicates an action or person deserves praise.

items.section: A · Suffix patterns and lexical creation
items.example: A productive suffix can still be used to create unfamiliar but understandable words.
items.note: Productive means available for creating new words; -able is productive but -ible generally is not.

items.pt: cunhar uma palavra; criar um termo
items.section: A · Suffix patterns and lexical creation
items.example: The researchers coined a word for the newly observed behaviour.
items.note: To coin a word means create a new lexical expression, not merely repeat a familiar term.

items.example: The debate became lively when participants challenged the evidence.
items.note: Ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb.

items.example: The company faced a costly delay after the redesign.
items.note: An adjective meaning expensive; not a manner adverb.

items.example: They took a leisurely walk along the riverside.
items.note: Usually an adjective suggesting a relaxed pace; can also be an adverb in some uses.

items.example: The miserly landlord refused to replace broken heaters.
items.note: Adjective for someone extremely unwilling to spend or share money; disapproving.

items.example: Every applicant must submit evidence of previous experience.
items.note: From apply; someone applying for a job, course or other opportunity.

items.example: The insurance claimant provided receipts for the damaged equipment.
items.note: Someone who formally claims a payment, right or benefit.

items.example: Investigators protected the informant's identity.
items.note: Someone supplying information, particularly to authorities; differs from informer in connotation and usage.

items.example: Each contestant had two minutes to present a solution.
items.note: A person taking part in a contest or competition.

items.pt: ocupante; pessoa que ocupa um imóvel
items.example: The occupant of the flat reported a faulty alarm.
items.note: A person using or living in a building, room or vehicle.

items.example: He wore a thick woollen jumper during the winter visit.
items.note: Adjective formed from wool; British spelling woollen, American often woolen.

items.example: The late sunlight gave the hills a golden colour.
items.note: Adjective from gold; literal or figurative.

items.example: Moisten the cloth before wiping the display.
items.note: Verb from moist: make slightly wet, not completely soak.

items.example: She prefers to sweeten her tea with honey.
items.note: Verb from sweet; can also mean make an offer or arrangement more appealing.

items.example: The delays may worsen unless additional staff arrive.
items.note: Verb from worse: become or make something worse.

items.example: His cheeks began to redden in the cold wind.
items.note: Verb from red, describing a change of colour.

items.example: Whether the evidence is conclusive remains a debatable issue.
items.note: -able can indicate that a question is open to discussion.

items.pt: preocupado com dinheiro; atento a custos
items.example: Money-conscious buyers compared the running costs first.
items.note: -conscious marks an area of attention; may imply careful spending.

items.example: The city introduced a car-free zone near the school.
items.note: Often describes an area where cars are not permitted.

items.example: The hikers packed energy-rich snacks for the climb.
items.note: -rich describes a high amount of energy or the stated component.

items.pt: liderado por franceses; sob liderança francesa
items.example: A French-led research consortium coordinated the trials.
items.note: Nationality adjective + -led; a hyphenated compound.

items.pt: voltado para esportes; interessado em esportes
items.example: Her sports-minded friends organised weekend matches.
items.note: The source exercise permits the variant sport-minded; sports-minded is also idiomatic.

items.example: The vehicle was fitted with bulletproof windows.
items.note: Means able to resist bullets; often spelled as one word.

items.pt: relacionado a drogas; relacionado a medicamentos conforme o contexto
items.example: The report separated drug-related offences from other crimes.
items.note: The context determines whether drug refers to illegal drugs or medicines.

items.example: The charity worked with several poverty-ridden communities.
items.note: Expresses an extreme negative condition; choose carefully in respectful writing.

items.example: The agency needed a trustworthy person to handle confidential records.
items.note: Worthy of trust; not the same as trustful, meaning inclined to trust others.

items.example: Oil-rich countries can still face serious fiscal challenges.
items.note: Rich in natural oil resources, especially petroleum.

items.example: His guilt-ridden expression made his discomfort obvious.
items.note: Common modifier-noun pairing in the exercise.

items.example: Each component must be clearly identifiable on the drawing.
items.note: Derived from identify + -able; able to be recognised.

items.example: The station installed vandal-proof ticket machines.
items.note: Resistant to vandalism; does not guarantee that damage is impossible.

items.example: They documented daily life in a terror-ridden region.
items.note: -ridden intensifies an oppressive negative circumstance.

items.example: Nutrient-rich soil helped the young trees grow.
items.note: A singular substance noun precedes -rich.

items.pt: com capacidade de obter crédito; digno de crédito financeiro
items.example: The bank judged the applicant creditworthy after checking his accounts.
items.note: In financial contexts, judged likely or able to repay loans.

items.example: The cafe offers a meat-free lunch every weekday.
items.note: -free indicates absence of meat; not necessarily free of animal products.

items.example: The study identified class-related inequalities in access to education.
items.note: The first noun is normally singular before -related.

items.example: They added vitamin-rich vegetables to the menu.
items.note: Indicates high vitamin content.

items.example: Check whether the fabric is dry-cleanable before buying it.
items.note: Can be cleaned by dry-cleaning; -able can attach to an established compound verb.

items.pt: preocupado com a aparência das roupas; atento à moda
items.example: The clothes-conscious presenter planned every outfit carefully.
items.note: A lexicalised exception in the exercise to the usual singular first element; retain clothes.

items.example: A government-led initiative expanded internet access.
items.note: A programme directed by government rather than by private groups.

items.example: Dampening the cloth reduced the amount of dust in the air.
items.note: Verb ending -en; can also mean reduce enthusiasm or force.

items.example: The receptionist offered a friendly welcome.
items.note: An adjective ending in -ly, not an adverb.

items.pt: profundamente; muito; a um preço alto
items.example: She dearly wanted the scholarship but knew it was competitive.
items.note: Here -ly marks an adverb; dearly also means at a high price.

items.example: The actor wore a silken scarf for the scene.
items.note: An adjective from silk with -en, often literary.

items.example: Sanding the surface lightly will roughen it.
items.note: Verb formed with -en from rough.

items.example: He delivered a masterly analysis of the constitutional problem.
items.note: Despite -ly, masterly is an adjective meaning extremely skilful.

items.example: A kindly neighbour looked after their cat during the trip.
items.note: Kindly can be an adjective meaning kind or an adverb meaning in a kind way.

items.example: Heavy clouds began to darken the sky.
items.note: Verb with -en indicating a change of state or colour.

units.title: Unit 88 — Word-building and word-blending
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 182–183 (PDF pages 184–185).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Word formation · classical roots, blends and derivation
learningObjectives: Infer meanings from common Greek- and Latin-derived word parts without assuming they are all productive.
Interpret and use academic, technology-related and sociocultural derived vocabulary.
Recognise established blends and identify how their component words contribute to meaning.
Apply word-family and derivation distinctions, including exercise-only academic and technology terms.

sectionsChecked: A · Common established word parts and Language help

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: The region became autonomous after negotiations with the central government.
items.note: auto- refers to self; autonomous means self-governing or acting independently.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: The laboratory tested biodegradable packaging under controlled conditions.
items.note: bio- relates to living things; biodegradable materials can break down through biological processes.

items.pt: cibercafé; estabelecimento com acesso à internet
items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: A cybercafé offered computer access before home broadband was common.
items.note: cyber- relates to computers and digital networks; the term is now less common in many places.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: Repeatedly dismissing suggestions can demotivate experienced staff.
items.note: de- can reverse or reduce the effect of a motivating action.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: He learned to balance on a monocycle as a child.
items.note: mono- means one; monocycle is an uncommon term, also called a unicycle.

items.pt: monografia; estudo aprofundado sobre um único tema
items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: She published a monograph on early computing history.
items.note: mono- means single and -graph- relates to writing.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: The international congress brought researchers together for three days.
items.note: -gress- derives from a root meaning to step or go; congress is an established term, not a freely formed compound.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: She chose to specialise in obstetrics after completing her medical training.
items.note: -ics can denote a field of study; obstetrics deals with pregnancy and childbirth.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: The course introduced phonetics before studying regional accents.
items.note: -phon- relates to sound and -ics to a field of study.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: His research in criminology examined the causes of repeat offending.
items.note: -ology means study; criminology is the study of crime and offenders.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: The visitor collected a prepaid ticket from reception.
items.note: pre- means before; prepaid is paid for in advance.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: The agreement included a retroactive pay increase.
items.note: retro- conveys backward reference; a retroactive measure applies to an earlier period.

items.pt: tecnofobia; medo ou aversão à tecnologia
items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: Technophobia can discourage people from trying unfamiliar software.
items.note: techno- relates to technology, while -phobia indicates fear or aversion.

items.section: A · Classical roots and word parts
items.example: In the novel, the twins appear to share a telepathic connection.
items.note: tele- means over a distance; this term describes supposed communication without normal sensory contact.

items.pt: brunch; refeição entre café da manhã e almoço
items.example: The delegates met for brunch after the morning session.
items.note: Blend of breakfast and lunch.

items.example: The hospital opened a heliport for emergency aircraft.
items.note: Blend combining helicopter and airport.

items.example: Thick smog reduced visibility across the city.
items.note: Blend of smoke and fog; describes polluted air that resembles fog.

items.pt: motel de beira de estrada; hospedagem para motoristas
items.example: They stayed at a roadside motel during the drive.
items.note: From motor and hotel; English motel is usually roadside accommodation, unlike the common Brazilian usage.

items.example: The research group held a webinar on data reproducibility.
items.note: Blend of web and seminar; an online presentation or seminar.

items.example: Our first budget was only a guesstimate, not a detailed forecast.
items.note: Blend of guess and estimate; informal and less precise than an evidence-based estimate.

items.example: The broadcaster produced a docudrama about the expedition.
items.note: Blend of documentary and drama; presents real events with dramatised scenes.

items.example: The officer used a breathalyser to estimate alcohol levels.
items.note: Blend of breath and analyser; British spelling, American breathalyzer.

items.example: The biography explores how the scientist developed her earliest theories.
items.note: bio- relates to life and -graph- to writing.

items.example: The actor delivered a dramatic monologue at the end of the play.
items.note: mono- means one; a long speech by one person.

items.example: The emergency telephone was located beside the lift.
items.note: tele- indicates distance; -phon- relates to sound.

items.example: Her autobiography covers her childhood and early career.
items.note: Written account of one's own life; auto- self, bio- life and -graph- writing.

items.example: The seminar focused on phonology and the organisation of speech sounds.
items.note: -phon- refers to sound and -ology to its study.

items.pt: regredir; voltar a um estado pior
items.example: Without further investment, the service may retrogress.
items.note: Means move backward, often toward an earlier less developed state; relatively formal or uncommon.

items.example: The candidate questioned the validity of graphology as a hiring tool.
items.note: Study or interpretation of handwriting; handwriting-based personality claims lack strong scientific support.

items.example: The sudden policy change could destabilise the coalition.
items.note: de- indicates reversal; British spelling destabilise.

items.example: The author signed an autograph for a reader after the lecture.
items.note: auto- means self and -graph- relates to writing; a person's handwritten signature.

items.example: The monotonous noise made concentration difficult.
items.note: Related to mono- meaning one; little variation in sound or activity.

items.example: Reliance on monoculture can increase vulnerability to crop disease.
items.note: Agricultural system relying on a single crop; mono- one.

items.example: A technocrat was appointed to oversee the economic reforms.
items.note: Person exercising authority largely on the basis of specialist technical expertise.

items.example: The technology improved image processing speed significantly.
items.note: techno- relates to practical technical knowledge and machines.

items.example: The committee considered the measure a retrograde step.
items.note: Formal adjective meaning moving backward or a return to an inferior state.

items.example: The museum organised a retrospective exhibition of her work.
items.note: Looking back at earlier events, achievements or work.

items.example: They observed the planet through a small telescope.
items.note: tele- distance, and -scope from a separate root meaning to look.

items.example: Modern telecommunications connect remote research stations.
items.note: Systems for transmitting information over distance.

items.example: The machine has an automatic shut-off function.
items.note: auto- conveys self-acting operation.

items.example: The exhibition traced the development of the automobile.
items.note: Auto- self and mobile moving; more formal or regional than car.

items.example: The archive contains several pre-war photographs.
items.note: pre- indicates before a particular war.

items.example: Pilots must complete a pre-flight inspection.
items.note: pre- indicates prior to a flight.

items.example: Postnatal care is essential for mothers and newborn babies.
items.note: post- denotes after; relating to the period after childbirth.

items.example: The committee decided to postpone the hearing until Friday.
items.note: An established word meaning delay until a later date; post- means after.

items.example: They collected biological samples for analysis.
items.note: bio- relates to living organisms.

items.example: Habitat destruction threatens local biodiversity.
items.note: The variety of living organisms within a particular area or ecosystem.

items.example: The novel contains several autobiographical details.
items.note: Based on the author's own life, though not necessarily a factual autobiography.

items.example: The speaker described autosuggestion as a self-directed mental technique.
items.note: Attempting to influence one's own beliefs or responses by repeated suggestions.

items.example: Teleworking became more common after improvements in internet access.
items.note: Working remotely while maintaining contact through telecommunications.

items.example: The region faced severe job losses during deindustrialisation.
items.note: A reduction in the scale or importance of industrial activity; British spelling.

items.example: Investigators traced the cybercrime to a compromised server.
items.note: Criminal activity involving computers or networks.

items.example: The aircraft was on autopilot during the routine part of the flight.
items.note: System that automatically controls an aircraft or other vehicle.

items.example: The school adopted procedures to report cyberbullying.
items.note: Bullying conducted through digital communication.

items.pt: pessoa com aversão à tecnologia; tecnófobo
items.example: He called himself a technophobe despite using a smartphone daily.
items.note: A person fearful of or strongly uncomfortable with technology; informal.

items.example: She presented preliminary results at a pre-conference workshop.
items.note: Describes a session or activity held before the main conference.

items.example: The postgraduate programme includes modules in health informatics.
items.note: Study of information processing and its applications; domain varies with context.

items.example: The late-night infomercial demonstrated several features of the appliance.
items.note: Blend of information and commercial; typically promotional rather than impartial information.

items.example: She recorded a podcast about new findings in astronomy.
items.note: Historically associated with iPod and broadcast; now commonly any downloadable or streamed episodic audio show.

items.example: The documentary crew borrowed an old camcorder for the project.
items.note: Blend of camera and recorder.

items.example: The restaurant added a veggieburger to its menu.
items.note: Blend of veggie and burger; spelling may also appear as veggie burger.

items.pt: maratona de natação; desafio de natação de longa duração
items.example: The community organised a swimathon to raise money for the hospital.
items.note: Blend of swimming and marathon; often a sponsored swimming event.

items.example: The researchers used freeware to annotate the images.
items.note: Blend of free and software; no purchase cost, but not necessarily open-source or free of restrictions.
